measurement.happened:
This week in Iraq was dominated by a cluster of court verdicts that will reverberate well beyond Baghdad. The single biggest story, covered by at least seven outlets across Reuters, AP, Deutsche Welle, and TV5Monde, was the sentencing of three to seven French nationals to life in prison for membership in the Islamic State. The TV5Monde headline in French confirms the same story: six French jihadists condemned to life. The numbers vary slightly between sources (three, six, or seven), which suggests the court may have handed down sentences in a single hearing covering multiple defendants, and different outlets counted the group differently. Either way, France now has a significant number of its own citizens locked up for life in an Iraqi prison, and that is going to be a diplomatic headache in Paris. The same week, AP reported that an Iraqi court also sentenced two politicians and an oil official in a graft case, so the judiciary was in full swing on high-profile convictions.

The seventh anniversary of the Tishreen protests fell on October 25, and Al Jazeera and Reuters both covered it. Reuters described slain protesters inspiring a wall of wishes, which tells you the memory is still raw and that the reform demands of 2019 have not been fully met. This is not a new uprising but a recurring pulse of public frustration that the government has to manage every October.

On the religious and cultural front, the Pope was in Mosul, where Reuters noted he freed a dove and prayed for the dead. Reuters also ran a piece on Iraq's Christians marking what they are calling a bittersweet first Christmas back home in areas they lost to the Islamic State. The Pope's presence and the Christian community's tentative return are part of the same narrative: Iraq is slowly stitching itself back together in the Christian heartland of the north, but the scars are very much present.

In security, Reuters reported that a drone was intercepted near Baghdad's Green Zone, the fortified compound housing the government and foreign embassies. It was not a massive attack, but a drone getting that close is a reminder that the airspace over Baghdad is not as clean as it would like to be.

Diplomatically, Al Jazeera reported that Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi met Ahmed al-Sharaa in what was described as a historic Syria visit. That is a significant signal that Baghdad is re-engaging with Damascus as a full partner, not just a neighbor across a porous border. This dovetails with the Reuters report that DNO is exploring exporting Kurdistan-region oil via Syria, which would be a major shift in how northern Iraqi crude reaches the Mediterranean, bypassing Turkey for at least part of the flow.

AP also reported that PKK-linked Yazidi militia units are set to disarm and join the Iraqi army, a push to consolidate weapons under state control in the north. That is a long, messy process, but the announcement itself is a political statement that Baghdad wants a unified military command.

Finally, the Wall Street Journal noted that the United States has allowed wind-down transactions with an Iran-linked Iraqi bank. This is a quiet but important financial signal: Washington is easing the screws just enough to let a specific transaction close, which suggests the broader sanctions architecture around Iraq is being recalibrated, possibly to give Baghdad more breathing room as it deepens ties with Syria and manages its own oil economics.
measurement.expected:
Theme: French diplomatic reaction. Almost certain that France will issue a formal statement, likely through the Quai d'Orsay, expressing concern over the life sentences and requesting consular access and a review of the cases. Possible that the French parliament will schedule a debate or that opposition parties will press the government for a diplomatic note. Unlikely that France will demand an immediate pardon within this one-week window, but expect the story to stay in French media.

Theme: Tishreen anniversary follow-through. Probable that the wall of wishes and reform demands will generate a few more local news stories and social media activity in the coming days, but the big public moment was October 25. Possible that one or two smaller demonstrations or sit-ins will pop up in Basra, Kirkuk, or Baghdad, especially if the government is perceived to be ignoring the anniversary. Unlikely that this triggers a full-scale new protest wave within a single week.

Theme: Corruption-case fallout. Probable that the two politicians and the oil official named in the AP graft story will file appeals or that their parties will issue statements. If one of the politicians is from a major bloc, expect a brief round of political posturing in parliament. Possible that the oil official's conviction stirs questions about the DNO pipeline deal with Syria, since the same sector is now under a cloud.

Theme: Pope and Christian community. Almost certain that the Pope's Mosul visit will continue to generate coverage and that local Christian parishes will hold small commemorative services in the coming days. The bittersweet first Christmas theme will keep Iraq's Christian community in the news through the end of the month, but no major new event is expected this specific week beyond continued media recaps.

Theme: Kurdistan oil via Syria. Possible that DNO or the Kurdistan Regional Government will issue a technical or logistical update on the pipeline feasibility study. Unlikely that a signed deal or groundbreaking happens within seven days, but expect at least one press release or interview confirming that talks are ongoing. The Iraq-Syria PM meeting gives this a political tailwind, so the story is likely to get a second wave of attention.

Theme: Security around Baghdad. Possible that the Green Zone drone interception prompts the Iraqi military to issue another brief statement or that a second low-level drone or missile is detected in the next few days, given the pattern of near-misses. Unlikely that a major attack on the Green Zone itself occurs this week, but the nervousness in Baghdad's security establishment will be visible in official statements.

Theme: PKK-linked Yazidi disarmament. Probable that the first logistical steps (rostering, equipment handover) are announced or that a small unit formally deploys to a new Iraqi army base. This is a slow process, so expect incremental news rather than a dramatic one-day event. Possible that a minor friction or disagreement between the Yazidi commanders and the Iraqi army staff makes a local headline.

Theme: Banking and Iran linkages. Possible that the WSJ wind-down story prompts a follow-up from the Iraqi central bank or the Ministry of Finance explaining the terms. Unlikely that a second Iran-linked bank gets a similar waiver this week, but the signal that Washington is selectively loosening up will be noted by regional financial press.

Less likely surprises: A snap parliamentary session called specifically to debate the French sentences or the corruption verdicts; a minor explosion or car-bombing in a Baghdad neighborhood that briefly dominates the news cycle; a surprise statement from the Iraqi foreign ministry welcoming or critiquing the Pope's visit; a brief power outage in Baghdad that gets blamed on a technical fault but stirs public grumbling.

Things I would not bet on: A full-scale new Tishreen-style uprising with tens of thousands in the streets; a major military clash between Iraqi forces and a PKK or Shia militia unit; the resignation of the prime minister or a cabinet reshuffle triggered by the corruption case; a second drone or missile actually hitting the Green Zone; a formal declaration of a new oil pipeline deal signed and announced; France pulling its ambassador from Baghdad; a new IS cell claiming a large attack in the north.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the center of gravity in Iraqi news shifted decisively from external security and economic positioning to domestic justice, religious reclamation, and regional reorientation. In the first photo, the dominant thread was the US troop drawdown and the security gap it leaves: a paramilitary base explosion, a border closure with Iran, and the Air France-KLM airspace fine all orbit the same question of who is watching Iraq's sky and ground. By the second photo, that thread has thinned to a single drone shot near the Green Zone and a quiet US bank wind-down permission. The drawdown is no longer the headline; it is the backdrop. What has grown into the foreground is the judiciary. The first photo had no court story at all. The second is saturated with them: French nationals sentenced to life for ISIS membership, two politicians and an oil official convicted in a graft case. The courts have become Iraq's most visible instrument of sovereignty, and the French verdicts in particular turn a domestic trial into a bilateral diplomatic event. A second new axis is religious and cultural. The Pope in Mosul, the freeing of a dove, Christians marking a bittersweet first Christmas in areas they lost to the Islamic State: none of this was present in the first photo, and it introduces a slow, tender narrative of return that sits in tension with the hard security stories. A third axis is Syria. The first photo had Iraq-Iran border friction as the regional thread. The second has the Prime Minister making what is called a historic visit to Damascus and DNO exploring a Kurdistan oil pipeline through Syria to the Mediterranean. Iraq is re-engaging with a neighbor it had largely sidelined, and the oil-route story suggests this is not just diplomatic posturing but a commercial bet. On the domestic-military side, the PKK-linked Yazidi militia disarmament announcement appears in the second photo and not the first, signaling Baghdad's push to consolidate weapons under a single command in the north. What has shrunk or vanished: the Sheeb border closure is gone from the headlines, implying it reopened or the story faded; the IMF program talks that were central to the first photo are silent in the second; the Anton/Chinese oil marketing story has no follow-up; the Dundee United football curiosity has disappeared entirely, as expected. The Tishreen seventh anniversary, which was not in the first photo, now punctuates the week as a recurring reminder that the 2019 reform demands are still unmet. In speed terms, the shift is fast: within eight days, the story moved from 'how do we survive without the Americans' to 'how do we try our own terrorists, welcome our Pope, and open a new oil road to the sea.'
delta.wind: Theme by theme, the expectations were directionally right about security but wrong about what would dominate. The forecast said the US troop withdrawal would continue to dominate and that at least one more incident at a paramilitary or military site would be reported. A drone was indeed intercepted near the Green Zone, so the security-incident expectation came true in a close form, but it was a single event, not a sustained narrative, and the drawdown itself was no longer the lead story. The expectation that the Sheeb border closure would remain in effect for the full week and that Baghdad would announce a formal security review or joint patrol with Iran before reopening appears to have been wrong: the closure is absent from the second photo, suggesting it lifted quietly without the predicted ceremonial statement. The forecast predicted follow-up commentary on the Air France-KLM fines, a US Treasury or State Department clarification, and possibly a new fine or a Paris diplomatic note. None of that appears in the second photo. The airspace story did not die but mutated: the drone near the Green Zone is the same anxiety, just a different incident. The IMF expectation was that technical staff would be in Baghdad and a preliminary framework would be announced by Friday or the weekend. The second photo is silent on the IMF, which means either the talks continued without a public milestone or the story was simply outpaced by the court verdicts. The Anton oil-marketing follow-up was expected but did not materialize as a separate headline; the oil story instead reappeared in a different form, with DNO exploring a Syria route for Kurdistan crude, which is related but not the same thread. The forecast said a full diplomatic row with Iran was unlikely and the crossing would reopen by week's end with an enhanced-security statement. The crossing likely did reopen, but the predicted statement did not make the headlines, so the expectation was half-right. The Dundee United story was flagged as a long shot and unlikely to make front pages, and it vanished as predicted. The less-likely surprises the forecast listed included a cabinet reshuffle triggered by the security vacuum, a pipeline strike near the Iran border, and a surprise ministerial visit to Washington or Tehran. None of those appeared. What the forecast did not anticipate, and what turned out to be the week's actual center of gravity, was the cluster of court verdicts. The French ISIS life sentences were not in the expectation at all, and they became the single most-covered story across at least seven outlets. The graft conviction of two politicians and an oil official was also absent from the forecast. The Pope's visit to Mosul and the Christian return narrative were not mentioned in the expectations, yet they occupied a significant share of the second photo. The Syria re-engagement, including the PM's visit and the DNO oil-route exploration, was not in the forecast either; the expectations had Syria largely absent and Iran as the regional focus. The Yazidi militia disarmament was also a new thread. The US bank wind-down transactions, while small, were not predicted. Taken together, the pattern of error is that the expectations over-weighted the US-Iraq security transition and the Iraq-Iran border as the two dominant axes, and under-weighted Iraq's domestic judiciary, its religious-cultural reclamation in the north, and its reorientation toward Syria. The forecast treated Iraq as a country reacting to an external withdrawal. The actual week showed a country actively using its own institutions, its own religious sites, and its own regional relationships to assert that it is not merely a vacuum left by the Americans but a state making its own moves. The expectations were not wrong about the facts; they were wrong about what would feel like the story to a reader. The drawdown is real, but it is no longer the only story, and the week's headlines say that Iraq is busy being a country rather than a country in transition.
delta.driver: The force pushing Iraq from the first photograph to the second is the country's attempt to fill the institutional and diplomatic space that the US drawdown is opening, not by waiting for a replacement patron but by activating its own tools: its courts, its churches, its borders, and its regional relationships. The judiciary is the clearest example. Trying French citizens for ISIS membership and convicting domestic politicians for graft are acts of sovereign assertion that say Baghdad will no longer defer to foreign governments or to its own elites; the courts are the stage where Iraq performs its independence. The Pope's visit to Mosul and the Christian community's tentative return are the same impulse in a softer register: Iraq is saying that the northern heartland is not a scar to be managed but a place to be reclaimed, and it is inviting the world to witness that reclamation. The Syria re-engagement, from the PM's historic visit to the DNO oil-route exploration, is the geopolitical expression of the same drive: rather than being a narrow corridor between Iran and Turkey, Iraq is repositioning itself as a hub with multiple doors, and Syria is one of them. The Yazidi militia disarmament is the military-administrative piece: consolidate weapons under Baghdad, reduce the number of armed actors, and present a unified state. The Tishreen anniversary underpins all of this as a reminder that the public is watching and that the reform demands of 2019 have not been fully answered, so every institutional move is also a political signal to the streets. The US is still present, in the drone, in the bank wind-down, in the background of the whole drawdown, but it is no longer the engine of the story. The engine is Baghdad's own desire to be seen as a functioning, sovereign, multi-confessional state that can try its own terrorists, welcome its own Pope, open its own oil routes, and command its own militias. That desire is what moves the country from one photograph to the next.

crystal.reasoning:
I start from the present picture and extend each theme along its visible motion, then correct for the pattern of error in our previous expectations.

The present picture is saturated with domestic institutional action: French nationals sentenced to life for ISIS membership, two politicians and an oil official convicted for graft, the Tishreen seventh anniversary still echoing, the Pope in Mosul freeing a dove, Christians marking a bittersweet return, a drone intercepted near the Green Zone, the PM making a historic visit to Damascus, DNO exploring a Kurdistan oil route through Syria, PKK-linked Yazidi units about to disarm, and the US quietly allowing wind-down transactions with an Iran-linked bank. The US drawdown is real but it is the backdrop, not the engine.

The motion tells me the center of gravity shifted from external security and the US withdrawal to Iraq's own institutions performing sovereignty. The courts became the stage. The religious-cultural thread in the north is new and tender. Syria replaced Iran as the regional axis. The Yazidi disarmament is a consolidation move. The Tishreen anniversary is a pulse, not a wave.

The wind tells me where I have been wrong. I over-weighted the US as the dominant frame; it is now background. I over-weighted the Iraq-Iran border; it has faded. I under-weighted the judiciary, the religious narrative, and the Syria re-engagement. The pattern of error is treating Iraq as a country reacting to an external withdrawal when it is actually a country actively using its own tools to assert that it is a functioning state. I correct by shifting my weight toward domestic institutions, the Syria axis, and the religious-cultural thread, and by treating the US as a quiet presence rather than the organizing narrative.

Now I extend each theme. The French verdicts are fresh. France will react diplomatically within days: a foreign ministry statement, possibly a parliamentary question, and behind the scenes a discussion of clemency or prisoner exchange. The exact number discrepancy (three, six, or seven) means the story is still being digested and a clarifying statement from Baghdad is likely. The graft conviction of two politicians and an oil official will trigger party-level reactions in parliament; the convicted politicians' allies will either defend or distance themselves, and there is a chance of a small follow-up probe or a pointed parliamentary question. This is not a cabinet crisis, but it is a reminder that the judiciary is now a political actor.

The Tishreen anniversary was October 25. The week after is when the political class must respond to the public mood. I expect a small government gesture: a salary adjustment, a new appointment to a protest-favored ministry, or a PM statement referencing the 2019 demands. Localized commemorations in Basra, Baghdad, or the Anbar are probable but unlikely to cross into organized protest. The memory is raw, but the public is not in revolt; they are watching.

The Syria re-engagement is the most dynamic new axis. The PM's visit was called historic, which means there is a joint narrative to be built. I expect a follow-up communique or working-group announcement within the week. The DNO oil-route story will get more technical detail: feasibility studies, a timeline, possibly a joint statement from DNO and the Syrian oil ministry. Turkey, which has been the traditional corridor for KRG crude to the Mediterranean, will react. A Turkish energy minister or the KRG's oil minister will issue a statement protecting the existing Turkey route. This is not a confrontation, but it is a commercial signal that the old two-door model (Turkey and Iran) is becoming a three-door model.

The Yazidi militia disarmament is announced but not yet executed. The process is slow and messy. I expect logistical details to emerge: where the units will be stationed, the timeline, which command they will report to. There is a small risk of friction with local Kurdish parties, particularly the KDP, who have built relationships with these units over years. A minor disagreement or a delay in the first handover is plausible. A full ceremony is less likely this week; the process is in its first administrative phase.

The Pope's visit to Mosul is over, but the narrative lingers. I expect follow-up media coverage, possibly a small interfaith gathering in Nineveh or Qaraqosh, and the Christian community's tentative return story to continue in a softer register. This is not a headline generator for a second week, but it is a background texture that colors how the north is discussed.

Security baseline: the drone near the Green Zone was a single event. The US is still drawing down, but the next major drawdown announcement is not imminent. I expect one small security incident in the coming week: another drone, a minor IED, or a patrol-level clash. Nothing major. The US bank wind-down transaction may generate a small follow-up: a second transaction, a Treasury clarification, or a brief mention in a broader sanctions update. The Sheeb border is likely open now; occasional friction but not a headline.

Economy: the DNO-Syria story is the most likely to generate a follow-up. The IMF is silent, which means the talks are continuing without a public milestone. The dinar is stable post-devaluation. The Anton/Chinese oil story has faded. I do not expect a major fiscal announcement this week. The oil price may fluctuate globally, but Iraq-specific economic news will be quiet except for the DNO thread.

What I would not bet on: a major cabinet reshuffle (the cabinet was just formed and the graft conviction is not a crisis); a new mass uprising (the Tishreen pulse is a reminder, not a wave); a major kinetic security incident (missile, large explosion, or coordinated attack); a formal US-Iraq security agreement or a major drawdown milestone; a pipeline strike or major oil infrastructure event; a surprise foreign leader visit beyond the Syria follow-up; a new ISIS major attack; or a constitutional amendment. The week is not a turning-point week; it is a consolidation and reaction week.

Less likely surprises the motion makes more probable: France seeking clemency or a prisoner exchange for the ISIS convicts (the diplomatic headache is real, and France has precedent); Turkey issuing a pointed reaction to the Syria oil route (it is a commercial threat); a minor Yazidi disarmament friction event (weapons do not simply disappear, and local loyalties are complex); the graft conviction triggering a small chain of parliamentary questions or a follow-up probe into another ministry. These are not high-probability events, but the motion of the week makes them more likely than they would be in a static picture.

Correcting for the wind: I do not lead with the US. I do not lead with Iran. I lead with the courts, the Syria axis, and the religious-cultural thread. The US is a quiet presence. Iran is a background neighbor. The story is Iraq being a country that tries its own terrorists, opens its own oil routes, and welcomes its own Pope. That is the frame, and I write the forecast in that frame.

One small incident is the baseline expectation: another drone detected over Baghdad, a minor IED on a road in Diyala or Anbar, or a patrol-level clash near the Iran border. Nothing will cross the threshold of a major attack. The US will remain a quiet presence: the bank wind-down transaction may generate a small Treasury follow-up or a second permitted transaction, but no major drawdown announcement is expected. The economy will be quiet except for the DNO-Syria thread. The IMF talks are continuing without a public milestone. The dinar is stable. The Anton/Chinese oil story has faded from the headlines. No major fiscal announcement is expected. The oil price may fluctuate globally, but Iraq-specific economic news will be limited to the DNO story and possibly a brief from the central bank on reserves.

What I would not bet on: a major cabinet reshuffle, a new mass uprising, a major kinetic security incident, a formal US-Iraq security agreement, a pipeline strike, a surprise foreign leader visit beyond the Syria follow-up, a new ISIS major attack, or a constitutional amendment. The week is a consolidation and reaction week, not a turning-point week.
crystal.headline: Iraq Sentences French ISIS Convicts as Syria Oil Route Takes Shape
emoji_reasons: The French ISIS life sentences and the domestic graft conviction make the judiciary the week's dominant story.
The DNO exploration of a Kurdistan oil route through Syria to the Mediterranean is the most consequential economic development.
The PM's historic visit to Damascus and the Pope's visit to Mosul both put Iraqi leaders and dignitaries in motion, marking a week of significant travel and re-engagement.
crystal.tldr: Next week in Iraq will be defined by the diplomatic fallout from the French ISIS life sentences, the first concrete follow-up to the PM's historic Syria visit and the DNO oil-route exploration, and a modest government response to the Tishreen anniversary. Security will be quiet, the Yazidi disarmament will enter its first bureaucratic phase, and the Pope's Mosul visit will linger as a background texture. The US is present but in the background; the story is Iraq using its own courts, its own oil, and its own regional relationships to assert that it is a functioning sovereign state.
crystal.eli5:
This week in Iraq, a court in Baghdad gave life sentences to a group of French people who joined the Islamic State years ago. France is now dealing with the awkward fact that it has a bunch of its own citizens locked up for life in an Iraqi prison, and both countries are talking about what to do. At the same time, another court convicted two Iraqi politicians and an oil official for taking bribes, which is making ripples in parliament.

The big new story is that Iraq's prime minister just went to Syria for what everyone is calling a historic visit, and now a company called DNO is looking into shipping oil from northern Iraq through Syria to the sea instead of going through Turkey like it always has. That is a big deal because it gives Iraq a new road to sell its oil and makes it less dependent on just one neighbor. Turkey is watching closely because its own pipeline business could be affected.

The seventh anniversary of the big protests in 2019 just passed, and people in the streets are still angry that the government has not fixed everything they asked for. The government is probably going to make a small gesture, like a pay raise or a new appointment, to show it is listening without giving up too much. In the north, a group of Yazidi fighters who used to work with the Kurdish parties are about to hand over their weapons and join the regular army, which is a slow and messy process but a sign that Baghdad wants one army, not several. The Pope was in Mosul a few days ago, and the Christian community there is cautiously coming back to towns they lost to ISIS, which is a hopeful but bittersweet story. Overall, the week ahead is about Iraq trying to show the world it is a country that can run its own courts, open its own trade routes, and manage its own people, without needing the Americans to do it for them.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A built its picture around five specific threads: the US drawdown and Sheeb border closure, the Air France/KLM aviation fines, the IMF program timeline, the Anton Chinese oil-marketing story, and the Dundee United football item. It also flagged a possible minor skirmish or drone incident and a joint patrol arrangement with Iran before the Sheeb crossing reopens. Looking at the actual week, A scored a clean hit on the drone: it predicted 'a possible chance of a minor skirmish or drone incident in the border zone,' and Reuters reported a drone intercepted near Baghdad's Green Zone. The general mood of a managed US exit also held, with the Wall Street Journal noting the US allowed wind-down transactions with an Iran-linked Iraqi bank, which fits A's picture of a security review and recalibration. The Dundee United story indeed faded, as A expected. However, A's more specific predictions largely missed: the Sheeb crossing was not reported as reopening with a joint patrol arrangement; the US State Department or Treasury did not issue a clarifying statement on no-fly rules; the Air France/KLM fines did not generate the follow-up A expected; and the IMF preliminary framework or press release was not clearly in the headlines. The Anton oil story partially connects to the DNO/KRG-oil-via-Syria headline, but A framed it as Chinese firms in the queue, which is a different angle. Most critically, A missed the single biggest story of the week: the sentencing of three to seven French nationals to life in prison for IS membership, covered by at least seven outlets. A also did not anticipate the seventh anniversary of the Tishreen protests (October 25), the Pope's visit to Mosul, the Iraqi PM's historic Syria visit, the PKK-linked Yazidi disarmament, or the graft-case sentencing of two politicians and an oil official. A's 'things I would not bet on' list (full-scale war, carrier strike group, dinar devaluation over five percent, surprise election, volcanic event) was all correct in that none of those happened. Overall, A captured the security-undercurrent mood and the drone incident, but its more specific and detailed predictions about Sheeb, aviation, and the IMF timeline did not materialize, and it missed several of the week's top stories.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B took a more measured, probability-weighted approach. It correctly identified the US drawdown as the backdrop and assigned a medium probability to at least one low-intensity security event, which was validated by the drone intercepted near the Green Zone. B's KRG prediction was a solid hit: it assigned a medium probability to a KRG-Baghdad story appearing, and the actual week delivered the DNO story about exporting Kurdistan-region oil via Syria, which is exactly the kind of KRG-oil-and-federal-budget coordination B anticipated. B also correctly noted that the Dundee United story would likely fade, and it was right that domestic politics was not in full rupture, even though the Tishreen anniversary and the graft-case sentencing kept the political judiciary in the news. B's IMF prediction (mission in Baghdad, preliminary statement on program terms) was not clearly confirmed in the headlines, and B's expectation that the Sheeb crossing would be lifted with a statement or extended with a deadline was not specifically reported. B's 'domestic politics in a lull' was partially contradicted by the Tishreen anniversary coverage and the high-profile graft sentencing, though B hedged by saying the cabinet would be in the news 'only if something specific went wrong, a ministry reshuffle, a budget dispute, or a policy announcement,' and the graft case and Tishreen pulse fit that loose framing. B also missed the French IS sentencing, the Pope's Mosul visit, the PM's Syria visit, and the PKK/Yazidi disarmament. Its 'would not bet on' list (major US/Israeli strike, no-confidence motion, major oil price shock, natural disaster, major scandal or resignation, dramatic protest) was mostly correct, though the graft sentencing could be read as a minor scandal and the Tishreen anniversary as a pulse of protest, neither of which crossed B's threshold. Overall, B's hits were cleaner and its misses were less over-specific than A's, and its probability calibration was more defensible.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts shared the same core instinct: the week would be a continuation of the US-drawdown-and-security thread rather than a dramatic break, and both correctly ruled out a full-scale war, a major natural disaster, and a surprise political rupture. Both scored a hit on a low-intensity security event (the drone near the Green Zone), and both correctly expected the Dundee United football story to fade. Both also missed the week's single biggest story, the French IS sentencing covered by at least seven outlets, as well as the Tishreen anniversary, the Pope's Mosul visit, the Iraqi PM's Syria visit, the PKK/Yazidi disarmament, and the graft-case sentencing. These shared omissions are significant, but the question is which forecast served a reader better as a picture of the coming week. A made more specific, concrete predictions (Sheeb reopening with a joint patrol, a US Treasury statement on no-fly rules, an IMF framework by Friday, a follow-up on the Anton Chinese oil story) and several of those specifics did not materialize, which made A's miss list longer and more visible.
